title: How to be a good guest in someone else's home
description: A good guest is not a perfect one. They are the one who notices the work hosting takes, shares it lightly, and leaves the house — and the friendship — in better shape than they found them.

body.heading: Arrive as a helper, not a project
paragraphs: The kindest guests reduce work instead of creating it. Arrive when you said you would, bring something that fits the household rather than something that needs immediate attention, and ask the only question that matters early on: “what can I do that would actually help?”

Then accept the answer. If your host says sit down and relax, that is the help they want — company, not a second kitchen manager. Helping against someone's wishes is just another task for them to manage.

body.heading: Read the house, join the house
paragraphs: Every home runs on quiet rules: shoes off at the door, phones away at dinner, early nights or late ones. A good guest spots the pattern in the first hour and joins it without commentary. You are not surrendering your personality; you are speaking the local language.

Offer the same grace in reverse when plans wobble. Hosts worry far more about small failures than guests ever notice them, and a guest who treats a burnt side dish as a story rather than a shortcoming gives the whole evening its ease back.

body.heading: Leave well
paragraphs: Strip the bed if you stayed over, or ask. Leave the bathroom tidy, the borrowed charger returned, and a thank-you that names something specific: the soup, the loan of the good chair, the story at midnight.
Specific thanks tells your host their effort was seen in detail, not just in bulk. It is the difference between a guest who was fed and a guest who was hosted — and hosts invite the second kind back.

takeaway: Notice the work, share it lightly, join the house's quiet rules, and thank your host for something specific.
